content: Is the "one year away" prediction for "sorry-free low-quality code" or "quality of a mathlib PR by an experienced contributor but before review" or "same quality as code that's passed review for mathlib" or "actually reviewed and merged in mathlib, with AI tools having helped reviewers do more review in the same amount of time"? Since (a) we already know FLT is true and (b) lots of the dependencies are clearly of more general use and mathlib-appropriate (actually I'd argue FLT itself is mathlib-appropriate), I think getting those dependencies into mathlib is a lot more interesting than getting them sorry-free.

My understanding from Math Inc was that their "one year away" prediction was "sorry-free code of arbitrary quality".

As you point out, the point of the FLT formalisation is not really "check it's true" (at the back of my mind I definitely do want to do this but I am 99.99% sure it's going to be fine). The point is "use this high-profile goal as an excuse to get some modern number theory into mathlib" which is why I will continue to work on the post-1980s stuff manually: I believe that a lot of the most important material mathematically is in that part of the argument. However AI will get better and I am hoping that we'll be able to use the 1970s/1980s stuff as an experiment and as a way to measure how useful AI-generated code is for library-building and how this changes as time goes on.
Well, for the AI companies it's "use work on/completion of this high-profile goal to attract investors and promote product", from a corporate pov.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Mazur (150 pages, 1970s)

Needs Neron models (300 pages, 1960s) and class field theory (200 pages, 1920), totalling 650 pages :)

Does this mean that human contributors should get out of the way in case Math Inc scoops FLT like they did to sphere packing?

Edit: I should be more clear about what I am asking. Is the post 1980 portion of the project still planned to be a human-led human-formalization or will it pivot to a human-led AI-formalization? If it is the latter, do you expect that you will need any human contributors other than yourself? If it is the former, is there any provision preventing AI companies from switching to the latter unilaterally when they are able to?

Well Math Inc is here to stay and it won't be long before there are other players in this space. As I tried to explain, my vision for what's going on hasn't changed. A human formalisation of the 1990s stuff, which to me still looks like something very doable by 2029, and this course has made/will make it very clear exactly what else needs doing.

The way I see it is as follows. What are the possible headline results? There is "AI formalises FLT" which is pretty awesome because it gives us a datapoint as to what AI can do. There is "humans formalise FLT modulo 1980s" which is great because it's (a) the first major goal of the project as far as I am concerned and (b) it opens up the door to "mathlib gets automorphy lifting theorem" which is another milestone.

And then there is "AI formalises FLT modulo 1980s" which I think is much harder to sell as a story because one interpretation is "AI does 10% of job" and as I've said already I won't merge such a PR on the basis that I don't then want to have to maintain AI-generated code for a year/multiple years while it does the 10x harder job of then doing all the 1980s stuff.

As we've seen already, you can't stop the tech companies from pointing their tools at anything. But you can ask what the point of spending money formalising random stuff is (and if you're optimistic it will get to the point where the situation is "point the machine at X and pay $1K per page and either end up with nothing because the human proof is too poorly-written/incorrect or with code containing no reusable artifacts which will break the moment you bump mathlib and you have to pay another large amount to fix it"). Once you have such a tool the big question is what to point it at. Those in possession of the tool and money can point it at whatever they like, and this is I think a likely future. Does that mean that humans should stop formalising? I'm not convinced it does. Human formalisation brings clarity, it brings better abstractions (module topology, compact Hausdorff rings, hardly ramified representations etc, all coming from FLT), and it makes the core maths library better.

I think that what is going to happen is that a bunch of AI-generated libraries will appear downstream from mathlib, and my impression is that many of them will be one-off projects ("we did this book/paper just to show that it could be done") which will then rot. If such a project is that paper you were refereeing then great, you paid to check that the results are correct and we can now discard the artifact. Such a tool would be useful to society but it would not be useful to mathlib. My goal with FLT is to be useful to mathlib.

I totally agree with you that human formalizations have way more value than AI formalizations (at least for now) but unfortunately academics (especially early career ones) are forced by the system to maximize academic credit gained instead of value produced. I would hope that these two usually align but in this particular case there would be little to none academic credit associated to being a stepping stone for AIs or to cleaning up slop code even if this is where the actual value is. I guess my question is whether you would recommend early career researchers to devote their time to projects like FLT that have strong interests from AI companies?

I think that I would encourage young researchers to devote their time to working on the important questions in the field. For me the important question in the field right now is figuring out how to get mathlib to the point where it understands what's happening at the frontier of all areas of mathematics. It is not so obvious to me what role autoformalisation plays in this because right now machines cannot generate code at a standard appropriate for mathlib. Conversely mathlib still cannot state the key definitions and theorems going on at the boundary of Langlands in a useful way (or indeed in any way at this point) and I believe that this is a necessary prerequisite for the future goal of machine-assisted research in Langlands. I've typed hard Langlands questions into an expensive language model and the results have been very poor; there's still a long way to go here.

I take this to mean that you think there will still be academic credit associated to advancing mathlib even if it is already “formalized” somewhere in a poor quality? It seems to me that this isn’t really the case in traditional mathematics where little credit is given to the reorganization or new proof of already proven results (unless e.g. that the new proof generalizes to some new result) but I would love to believe that things are different here.

I think the situation is pretty clear: AI companies, and especially MathInc, will indeed thoroughly bomb this area to turn it in a giant radioactive wasteland that will never be able to sustain life again, so we will never get the benefits expected from formalization (improved understanding and accessibility). I strongly advise young people to contribute to less shiny projects that are less likely to be destroyed.

Us in the community might value this, but good luck getting a paper published or a grant for something like this. In Sphere packing we've already seen people get left without a masters Bsc project to work on or lose interest in continuing working on their PRs since it was done by Gauss and I don't blame them at all.

My understanding is that the humanities tend to give more academic status to publishing books that may largely be putting together new viewpoints on existing material, compared to sciences with a focus on new research papers. Maybe mathematics needs to become more like the humanities in terms of academic status for deeper understanding of existing material, while at the same time more like experimental sciences in terms of funding (all that AI compute will cost a lot of money)?

Lack of status associated with infrastructure work (software, databases, etc. - things needing ongoing maintenance and development rather than producing a research paper and then being done) is of course hardly new or restricted to formalization.

I think that "AI in collaboration with humans produces 10 high-quality mathlib PRs each of 200 lines of code, for one small part of one FLT dependency, and interacts with the community in review of those PRs" would be a much more interesting and valuable contribution than "AI produces a big dump of 10 million lines of low-quality code that provides a sorry-free proof of FLT, without community discussion of the approaches taken to developing definitions and theory and without PRing all the little lemmas and larger definitions along the way".

Like many people in the Lean community, I'm not impressed with how many of these AI companies operate. But as said above - these companies are not going to disappear anytime soon.

There is a lot of talent in the Lean community, and I think that most people will agree with me that the human contributions are more valuable (currently) than AI. So if people are stopping formalising results because some AI has produced a low-quality version of it, this tells me that we are losing the communication battle. I personally think this is a battle best fought collectively rather than as individuals with e.g a position statement which outline things like what is the value of human formalisations currently, what is the role of this skill set in the future etc... without speculation or hype.

As I've noted elsewhere, mathematical community values are essentially collaborative, and when AI developers take all the human mathematics literature, but then fail to respect community values (respecting collaborative values includes being open about the workings of their AIs and providing all information needed for other AI developers to replicate the work and build on it with their own ideas, and for mathematicians to dig into the workings of the AI to understand better how it does what it does), I think this is essentially cultural appropriation.

Is this a reason to consider being less transparent about the work happening in FLT or other higher profile projects, until that work is completed? My understanding is that a decent portion of the work involved for FLT specifically is in tying together long papers, many with explanation gaps or minor errors which need some resolving. If a group of experts go off in a room and formalize and only come back when a self-contained bit of work is finished and formalized, does this reduce the likelihood that some AI "picks off" the refined and synthesized papers/proofs and scoops autoformalizing them, and if so is the sacrifice there (of the virtues of openness) worth it to ensure those working on it get the credit?
Okay, this really needs a new topic, we're moving well past an "FLT update discussion".

Honestly, I think that would help, and is probably a good idea. I will also say that this idea makes me very sad.

I'm new to the field. I've been benefiting greatly from the (very generous) openness of projects like these. It's been incredibly motivating to make contributions, no matter how small, to real exciting work being spearheaded by expert mathematicians. I don't take that for granted at all -- I'm well aware that busy people are putting in extra time and effort to make things public, accessible, and open to collaboration from people new to the space. I assume their motivation is to grow the space, attract more talent to it, and invite collaboration from everyone interested regardless of their expertise.

I've also had the experience, more than once, of having something I was excited to get done sniped by some AI tool. I can't even claim that my code would necessarily have been better than what AI produced -- in my case, the only benefit of a human doing the work is that I would've learned something along the way and gone to bed happy about it. And while I know I could've pretended AI hadn't already solved it, I'm simply less motivated when I know I'm not going to feel like I "did something". There's a reason this is more exciting than simply working on exercises in a textbook.

That's why I'm mostly thinking about this as "I'm sad about it", and not "I think this will kill the space".

  • Before publication, significant restructuring of the AI's output into mathlib's style and a mathlib-like folder system
  • At publication, identification of gaps or deficiencies in mathlib's web of declarations, with corresponding upstreaming PRs

our response should be to publicly denounce said company for taking away motivation from potential human formalisers.

Again let me stress that they're not there yet. However 2 years ago I'm not sure they would have been helping me write my technical FLT lectures, and right now they are definitely very helpful. The fact that I know a lot about the FLT material means that I can ask a machine when I can't follow an argument which Taylor only sketches and the machine is good at having a go at filling in the details; when I know it's talking nonsense I just tell it and then it tries again. The machine has to convince me and I am careful. I find that I get a lot out of the collaboration.

For scientists and engineers, these autoformalization tools might become indispensable, since learning Lean is harder for non-mathematicians. (Saying this makes me feel like those people who think making art is hard, so they use AI to make art without taste). But I can imagine a future where one of these AI companies serves a product to a scientist where they interact informally with an autoformalization system that builds a world of Lean under the hood, and reports back to the scientist in natural language, asking for clarity or highlighting assumptions they might not have made explicit before. What of the quality of the formalization, beyond correctness? But also, what if this catalyzes their interest in Lean, and they want to look under the hood and start learning Lean? But also, what would motivate them (beyond idle curiosity) to learn something they saw as “solved” by AI?

Should any AI-developing company publish a Lean proof of any big mathematical result (e.g. the 2014 proof of the Willmore conjecture) without doing either of the following:

  • Before publication, significant restructuring of the AI's output into mathlib's style and a mathlib-like folder system
  • At publication, identification of gaps or deficiencies in mathlib's web of declarations, with corresponding upstreaming PRs

our response should be to publicly denounce said company for taking away motivation from potential human formalisers.

A code of conduct for large autoformalization projections needs to start long before those points. For example:

  • Plans must be disclosed in public before the project starts.
  • Respect any requests to avoid particular pieces of mathematics that someone else is working on formalizing, or plans to formalize, or plans to give to a student to work on formalizing, etc. (this doesn't imply a veto forever; the people with plans on those pieces of mathematics need to keep the community updated on their work as well, including if they are no longer working / planning to work on them).
  • Keep the public informed in detail about progress as you go along; no large code dumps or surprises from large pieces of work done in secret before release.
  • Autoformalizers used for large projects should be designed to identify and contribute the many small lemmas in loosely-related existing parts of mathlib (filling API gaps) that any human formalization beyond the smallest tends to produce.
  • Autoformalizers used for large projects should be designed to aim for quality not quantity (the quality of a mathlib PR submitted by an experienced contributor, before review, is a reasonable goal to aim for, since we don't expect any higher quality than that from humans), and for mathlib contribution wherever reasonable. (We already have the demonstration from sphere packing that autoformalizers can produce large code dumps needing a lot of work for integration. Demonstrating it once may have been useful, but now that's been demonstrated once, I think the value of demonstrating it again for a different piece of mathematics is negligible compared to the cost.)
  • Developers of autoformalizers should respect collaborative mathematical community values (mathematicians may find it hard to explain exactly how they came up with certain ideas sometimes, but if they know how they did so, they don't treat it as a secret when people ask, even if it's common for mathematical papers to present only the prettiest version of an argument without showing the inspiration). Building mathematics and mathematical libraries is not a zero-sum game. Developers of other AIs need to be treated as friends to collaborate with. People interested in understanding how your AI works need to be supported with all the technical information needed to replicate and study it, rather than treating the AI workings as some kind of trade secret (there are surely insights about how to prove things that could be mined from AIs that prove things). Certainly in the open source software world where I've worked for decades, when there are multiple alternative pieces of software in some area, each benefits from the existence of the others and cross-fertilization of ideas, and both developers and users benefit from this and from talking to those working on other such software about their choices and ideas.

  • A mathlib-quality autoformalization is usable and maintainable in ways that a low-quality one isn't.
  • It avoids the concerns about existence of a low-quality formalization of some piece of mathematics making it less likely we'll ever get a high-quality formalization of that mathematics now an AI company is claiming it as "done".

But there are several other things it doesn't address:

  • All the reasons given for autoformalization avoiding pieces of mathematics that people are working on or planning to work on still apply (there's plenty of other mathematics without such plans available for autoformalizers). So they need to announce their plans in public well in advance to find out about other work that would provide a reason to avoid a particular autoformalization project - and this includes all the significant subprojects for dependencies that might also have someone working or planning to work on them. And they should talk in advance to the authors of the papers they're thinking of autoformalizing (if the authors still available, obviously that can't be done for papers from 100 years ago) in case they know of such work or have other useful advice.
  • A formalization project is most useful if it puts all relevant code (non-leaf material likely to be of use to other projects) in mathlib, so autoformalization projects should aim for that as well, PRing everything appropriate along the way, both all the small additions to existing parts of mathlib that are naturally found as part of any medium or large formalization project (a good autoformalizer ought to try to extract such API pieces) and all the new definitions / API / theory as well.   • mathlib-quality doesn't just apply to the code, mathlib-quality community interaction is important as well. Apart from discussing proposed projects in public in advance as noted above, that includes doing the autoformalization in public rather than with large code dumps after private development, and engaging the community in discussion of whatever design questions arise (about how to design the API for some area of mathematics being developed as part of the autoformalization, etc.), as well as PRing things to mathlib and helping review others' PRs in related areas.
  • A large mathlib-quality formalization is more than just a large number of smaller pieces of mathlib-quality code; it generally results in insights into the underlying mathematics and how best to represent it in Lean (possibly through seeing common pain points in the formalization, or similarities to issues arising in other formalizations, or things that look in spirit like they are duplicative and ought to build on more common lemmas and definitions than they do). This is a fascinating distinction to make. You are trying to capture the delta between "the Lean kernel didn't throw an error" (which an AI can brute-force with thousands of lines of unreadable code) and "the Lean community recognized this as elegant, reusable, and foundational math."

Since the verb needs to fit smoothly into the sentence "The AI [Xed] sphere packing" (acting as a direct stand-in for "published"), here are the best single-word options broken down by the exact nuance they project:

To Emphasize Anti-Bloat and Mathematical Elegance

If your primary goal is to contrast the achievement against ugly, bloated, or brute-forced AI proofs, these words highlight the refinement required for Mathlib.

  • Canonicalized: This is arguably the strongest fit. In mathematics and computer science, a "canonical" form is the standard, simplest, or most natural representation. Saying "The AI canonicalized sphere packing" implies it didn't just solve it; it found the perfect, standard form that the community adopted.

  • Systematized: This conveys that the proof wasn't a one-off hack, but was organized and structured in a way that fits beautifully into a broader system (Mathlib's existing architecture).

  • Distilled: This is a slightly more poetic choice that directly combats the idea of "bloat." It implies the AI (or human) took a massive, complex mathematical truth and reduced it to its purest, most elegant, Mathlib-ready essence.

To Emphasize the Prestige and the "Canon"

If your goal is to make the achievement sound like a historic academic milestone—equivalent to landing in Annals of Mathematics—these words carry that weight.

  • Canonized: This packs a massive punch. It implies the theorem has been elevated from a mere working proof into the official, universally recognized "truth" of the formalized math world.

  • Enshrined: Similar to canonized, this carries a strong sense of legacy. It implies the proof was of such high quality that it has been permanently preserved in the Mathlib vault for future generations.

The "Insider" Choice

While you mentioned wanting a traditional academic sound, I have to offer the word that the formalization community actually uses as their highest badge of honor.

  • Upstreamed: In the culture of Lean (and heavily pushed by figures like Kevin Buzzard), "upstreaming" is the holy grail. Anyone can write a messy proof in a local repository. To "upstream" it means you successfully navigated the grueling peer-review process of the Mathlib maintainers, proved your code was general and maintainable, and got it accepted into the master library. Saying "The AI upstreamed sphere packing" instantly signals to anyone in the field that the proof was of human-expert quality.

The Verdict

If you want the strongest bridge between traditional academic prestige and the specific "clean code" standards of Mathlib, "canonicalized" or "canonized" are your best options. If you want to signal deep understanding of the formalization community's actual culture, use "upstreamed." Here is a more full-form version of a definition (again probably needs a lot of work), trying to include ideas people mentioned above:

A peer-reviewed formalisation

Within the context of Lean, a peer-reviewed formalisation is Lean code which has been deemed satisfactory by an independent named (directly or by association with an established body) Lean expert in the following areas: 

  1. Reusability: For example, how easy the code is to be used by another user.
  2. Organisation: For example, if theorems and definitions appear in the right place within the file. 
  3. Readability: How easy the code is to read by a Lean expert.
  4. Accuracy: For example, if the code represents the the results it is claimed to.
  5. Proof structure: Whether the proof structure is easy to follow, concise and where appropriate are split into lemmas
  6. Generality: For example, if the results are at an appropriate level of generality for the task at hand. 
  7. Motivation of form: The motivation for a particular form of a result is well thought through and where appropriate other experts consulted. 
  8. Integration: An appropriate level of effort has been put in to integrate the results into existing libraries where appropriate.
  9. Citations: The appropriate citations are included within the formalisation to used work in the same area.

Regarding large human projects and upstreaming into mathlib:

  • In many cases such projects give insights into what approaches work best for formalizing certain kinds of mathematical objects or arguments, even if the conclusion is that large pieces of the project would best be redone in a different way to get them into mathlib. We don't know how to extract such insights from formalizations by an AI that might be happy to repeat awkward arguments thousands of times rather than making everything cleaner by starting with a different API setup. (Which makes designing AIs to produce such insights an interesting research project, but not one that produces catchy headlines.)
  • Even if a lot of new material from the project isn't upstreamed, the human maintainers will hopefully have PRed many small lemmas and API additions for existing parts of mathlib as they went along (and such small API additions are often easier to get reviewed quickly). AIs don't seem good at identifying "this bit of this proof shows up an API gap in an existing part of mathlib, let's PR a general version right now before going further, and then I don't need to maintain it any more after I next update mathlib in my project".   • By doing the project in public at human speeds and discussing design questions with the wider community on Zulip when they seem possibly more generally relevant, a project can result indirectly in mathlib improvements of relevance to other projects even if it's not the direct source of those things being added to mathlib.
  • Apart from mathematical and scientific norms, there are open source development norms to consider. This is especially an issue for early career academics.

Math doesn't rely on replication the same way a lab science does, but we do need replication in the sense of novel and improved expositions, new approaches to known problems, and active dissemination of this information. How many algebraic geometers here read EGA and SGA as their first text of algebraic geometry? You probably read Hartshrone, Vakil, or Shafereveich. These books don't necessarily include shiny new theorems, but they do make the material accessible to newer generations and these resources clarify it for people that have already seen it and this is so important! I have benefitted immensely from expository works written by mathematicians that received no formal reward for doing said work.

I would argue that if an AI produces uninterpretable unmanageable code than it is actually still valuable to build out high-quality alternatives to this. That way the community can digest the formalization and it's human readable, we can see different approaches, the people who do this labor deepen their understanding to share with others, and we build out high-quality libraries for future use.
